cases.abstract: Collecting manipulation demonstrations across diverse scenes calls for a collection process that can vary environments while keeping robot control reproducible. We present DROID, a distributed dataset and shared collection platform deployed at 13 institutions. Collectors use portable Franka Panda hardware, calibrated cameras and VR teleoperation; scene-specific task sampling and periodic environment changes are used to broaden coverage. The resource provides 76,000 successful episodes, with 564 scenes and 350 hours reported for the collection, alongside collection and policy-training resources. We evaluate its utility with existing language-conditioned diffusion policies on six tasks in four locations using DROID hardware. DROID co-training mixes successful dataset trajectories equally with in-domain demonstrations and is compared with in-domain-only training and equal-mixture co-training using curated Open X-Embodiment data, with a shared policy backbone. With ten rollouts per method and task setting, DROID co-training exceeds the next-best method in across-task mean success rate by 22 percentage points in-distribution and 17 under out-of-distribution changes. These comparisons support supplementary training with DROID for the evaluated tasks and scene shifts, rather than replacement of in-domain demonstrations.
cases.methods: DROID uses a common Franka Panda platform so distributed collectors can change scenes without changing the robot control setup. Collectors use VR teleoperation with two adjustable external stereo cameras and a wrist stereo camera. At each new scene, collectors calibrate cameras and specify feasible tasks, from which an episode's task is sampled randomly. Periodic prompts ask collectors to vary camera placement, lighting, clutter or base position to broaden coverage. To assess successful DROID trajectories as supplementary training data, we train a separate language-conditioned diffusion policy for each of six tasks on DROID hardware. DROID co-training combines these trajectories and in-domain demonstrations in equal proportions. Comparators retain the backbone but use either in-domain demonstrations alone or an equal mixture with curated Open X-Embodiment data. Ten rollouts per method and task setting evaluate perturbed in-distribution initial positions and task-specific out-of-distribution changes across four locations.
cases.results: On six tasks evaluated with DROID hardware, combining successful DROID trajectories and in-domain demonstrations in a 50/50 mixture yields higher across-task mean success rate than in-domain-only training or 50/50 co-training with a curated Open X-Embodiment mixture using the same policy backbone. The margin over the next-best method is 22 percentage points in-distribution and 17 for task-specific out-of-distribution variants, with ten rollouts per method and task setting. Reported error bars are standard errors of the across-task mean. A separate comparison fixes both subsets at 7,362 successful demonstrations and retains 50/50 in-domain co-training: a uniformly sampled, more scene-diverse subset outperforms the subset from the 20 most represented scenes on the challenging out-of-distribution tasks studied. This size-matched check supports a role for scene diversity rather than dataset size alone, without isolating all other differences. Together, the comparisons support DROID as additional training data within these tasks and scene changes.

notes.abstract: Plan: connect varied collection to shared control (D01-D04, D09), then test supplementary-data utility (D05-D07). Read-back: platform and data remain distinct contributions; the gains retain their task average, rollout denominator and in-domain co-training scope.
notes.methods: Plan: follow scene setup through sampling to the training-data comparison (D01-D02, D05-D07). Read-back: collection choices explain intended coverage, while the shared backbone distinguishes data regimes without implying a new learning algorithm.
notes.results: Plan: test supplementary-data utility, then scene diversity at fixed subset size (D06-D08). Read-back: success rates are task averages with standard errors around their means; the secondary comparison supports diversity's role without isolating every confound or inheriting the main rollout count.

cases.abstract: Simulation can inform comparisons of robot policies trained on real data only if control and visual differences do not obscure their relative performance. We introduce SIMPLER, a simulated evaluation framework that targets policy ranking rather than exact reproduction of real-world success rates. Existing demonstration actions are replayed to tune simulated controllers against real end-effector motion. Visual Matching then combines simulated robots and interactive objects with an inpainted real-scene background and adjusted textures. Mean Maximum Rank Violation (MMRV) scores ranking errors by their real-world success-rate margins, emphasizing consequential reversals. For six policy checkpoints across three Google Robot task groups, Visual Matching achieves average MMRV of 0.056, compared with 0.143 for Variant Aggregation and 0.375 for rankings derived from validation action mean squared error. WidowX task comparisons yield task-averaged MMRV of 0.014, extending the ranking check to a second tested setup. The open-source release includes environments and construction guidance. The agreement supports relative policy evaluation in the tested, mainly rigid-body setups, not exact reproduction of every policy's success rate.
cases.methods: SIMPLER evaluates policies trained on real data in SAPIEN environments for Google Robot and WidowX, mainly on rigid-body tasks. To align action effects, we replay existing demonstration actions in simulation and tune controller stiffness and damping by simulated annealing against real end-effector translation and rotation. Visual Matching addresses appearance discrepancies by compositing segmented simulated robots and interactive objects onto an inpainted real background, then adjusting or projecting textures. Variant Aggregation instead averages outcomes over randomized visual variants. Paired real and simulated policy evaluations test whether these approaches preserve relative performance. Mean Maximum Rank Violation assigns each policy its largest real-world success-rate margin among simulator misrankings and averages those penalties across policies; lower values indicate closer ranking agreement. Pearson correlation provides a complementary measure of linear association rather than an interchangeable ranking score.
cases.results: Visual Matching provides closer agreement with real-world policy rankings than either Variant Aggregation or validation action mean squared error across six policy checkpoints and three Google Robot task groups. Average Mean Maximum Rank Violation, which weights ranking reversals by real-world success-rate margins and is lower when agreement is better, is 0.056, compared with 0.143 and 0.375, respectively. Mean Pearson correlations are 0.924, 0.778 and 0.308 in the same order. This comparison favors the matched simulator as a relative policy-evaluation signal rather than treating validation action error as an equivalent proxy. A separate robustness check moves beyond aggregate ranking: simulation suggests greater arm-texture sensitivity in Octo-Base than RT-1-X, and new real-world arm-wrapping experiments support that relative difference. The correspondence therefore includes a tested policy-dependent response to visual change, while remaining evidence about rankings and behavior in these setups, not exact success-rate reproduction.

notes.abstract: Plan: retain evaluation framework, gap-reduction operations and margin-aware ranking metric (S01-S05), supported by Google Robot and WidowX comparisons (S07-S08). Read-back: the numerical claims concern ranking agreement in tested setups; release scope remains mainly rigid-body evaluation (S10).
notes.methods: Plan: connect control alignment and appearance construction to paired ranking evaluation (S02-S06). Read-back: existing demonstrations tune action effects, not replacement policies; MMRV aggregates each policy's worst margin, while Pearson correlation measures a distinct relationship.
notes.results: Plan: compare ranking proxies (S07), then check a simulated visual sensitivity against hardware (S09). Read-back: task-group averages are agreement measures, not success rates; the arm-wrapping comparison supports the specific relative sensitivity, not arbitrary simulator fidelity (S01, S10).
